subject: chem
title: Equilibria
subtitle: Dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle and Kc.
concept: A dynamic equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse rates are equal, and concentrations remain constant.
Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, it responds to oppose that change.
The equilibrium constant Kc depends only on temperature; it is unaffected by concentration, pressure, or catalysts.

notes.heading: Dynamic Equilibrium
items: A dynamic equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. Concentrations remain constant — but both reactions continue to occur at the molecular level.

The equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^n / [reactants]^m, where the concentrations are raised to their stoichiometric coefficients. Only species in solution or the gas phase are included — pure solids and liquids are not.
The value of Kc depends only on temperature. A large Kc (>> 1) indicates products are favoured; a small Kc (<< 1) means reactants predominate.

notes.heading: Le Chatelier's Principle
items: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, it responds to oppose that change and restore equilibrium.
Concentration: adding a reactant shifts equilibrium toward products; removing a product has the same effect.
Pressure (for reactions involving gases): increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas.

Temperature: increasing T shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction. For an exothermic reaction, higher T decreases Kc (and the equilibrium yield of products). This is the only factor that changes the numerical value of Kc.
Catalyst: increases the rate of both forward and reverse reactions equally — equilibrium is reached faster, but the position and Kc are unchanged.

notes.heading: Industrial Applications
items: Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, exothermic): uses 450 °C (a compromise — lower T gives higher Kc but too slow a rate even with the Fe catalyst; 450 °C is the economic optimum), 200 atm (shifts toward fewer moles of gas, increasing yield), and Fe catalyst. Ammonia is continuously removed to shift equilibrium right.
Contact process (2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, exothermic): 450 °C, 1–2 atm (high yield is achievable at low pressure — high pressure equipment is not cost-effective), V₂O₅ catalyst.

definitions.body: The state in a closed system where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it responds so as to oppose the change and restore equilibrium.
The equilibrium constant in terms of concentrations; Kc = product of concentrations of products (raised to stoichiometric powers) divided by product of concentrations of reactants.

workedExamples.q: Write the Kc expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) and give its units.

steps.text: Units = (mol dm⁻³)² / [(mol dm⁻³)(mol dm⁻³)³] = mol⁻² dm⁶

workedExamples.q: The Haber process is exothermic. Explain the effect of increasing temperature on yield and Kc.

steps.text: Increasing T favours the endothermic direction — the reverse reaction — shifting equilibrium to the left.
Kc decreases (the equilibrium lies further to the reactant side at higher T).

mistakes: Including pure solids (e.g. CaCO₃) or pure liquids in the Kc expression.
Saying a catalyst shifts the equilibrium position — it does not.
Confusing the effect of temperature on equilibrium position with the effect on rate.
tips: Always state which direction the equilibrium shifts AND the effect on yield/concentration.
For Kc units: if top power equals bottom power, Kc is dimensionless (no units).
Industrial compromise temperatures: high enough for acceptable rate, but Kc still reasonable.

flashcards.a: Forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations are constant; the system is closed.

flashcards.q: What is the only factor that changes the value of Kc?
For an exothermic reaction, what happens to Kc when temperature increases?
flashcards.a: Kc decreases — equilibrium shifts to the endothermic (reverse) direction.

flashcards.q: How does increasing pressure affect an equilibrium with fewer moles of gas on the right?
flashcards.a: Increases the yield of products — equilibrium shifts to the right (fewer moles of gas).

flashcards.q: Does a catalyst affect Kc or equilibrium position?
flashcards.a: No — a catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse rates equally; it does not change Kc or equilibrium position.

flashcards.q: Write the Kc expression for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), what happens when pressure is increased?
opts: Equilibrium shifts right; more NO₂ formed
Equilibrium shifts left; more N₂O₄ formed
questions.exp: Increasing pressure favours fewer moles of gas — the left side (1 mol vs 2 mol), so N₂O₄ is favoured.

questions.q: A reaction has Kc = 1×10⁻⁸. What does this indicate?
opts: Equal amounts of reactants and products
questions.exp: Very small Kc means the equilibrium lies far to the left — reactants are strongly favoured.

questions.q: Which correctly shows Kc for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃?
questions.exp: Kc = [SO₃]² / ([SO₂]²[O₂]) — products over reactants, raised to stoichiometric powers.

questions.q: An endothermic equilibrium is heated. What happens?
opts: Kc decreases; yield of products falls
Kc increases; yield of products rises
questions.exp: Increasing T for an endothermic reaction shifts equilibrium right; Kc increases.

questions.q: Why is a lower temperature not used in the Haber process despite giving higher Kc?
opts: Rate would be too slow to be economical
questions.exp: Lower T gives higher equilibrium yield (Kc larger) but unacceptably slow rate — a compromise temperature ~450°C is used.

summary.value: no effect on Kc or position
